title: fanoutqa: Who are the Nobel Prize winners in Physics from the year 2010 to 2015? Provide a brief description of their contributions. (14b8f8068a304024)

chat_history.content: Who are the Nobel Prize winners in Physics from the year 2010 to 2015? Provide a brief description of their contributions.

content.content:
We need list of Nobel Prize winners in Physics for years 2010-2015 inclusive. Provide brief description of contributions.

We can answer from knowledge. Let's recall:

2010: Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov – Nobel for graphene. Contributions: isolation of single-layer graphene, discovery of its extraordinary properties.

2011: Saul Perlmutter, Brian P. Schmidt, and Adam G. Riess – Nobel for discovery of accelerating expansion of the universe via distant supernovae.

2012: Sergei G. Kovalev? Actually 2012 Physics Nobel: Steven Chu, Claude Cohen-Tannoudji, and William D. Phillips – for development of methods to cool and trap atoms with laser light.

2013: François Englert and Peter W. Higgs – Nobel for theoretical discovery of mechanism that gives mass to elementary particles (Higgs mechanism).

2014: Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano, and Shuji Nakamura – for development of blue LEDs.

2015: Takaaki Kajita and Arthur B. McDonald – for discovery of neutrino oscillations, demonstrating neutrinos have mass.

Double-check 2012: Yes, Steven Chu, Claude Cohen-Tannoudji, William D. Phillips. Good.

Also 2010 winners: Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov; 2011: Saul Perlmutter, Brian P. Schmidt, Adam G. Riess; 2012: Steven Chu, Claude Cohen-Tannoudji, William D. Phillips; 2013: François Englert, Peter W. Higgs; 2014: Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano, Shuji Nakamura; 2015: Takaaki Kajita, Arthur B. McDonald.

Provide brief description of contributions. We'll mention the significance.

We may also note that the Nobel Prize is awarded to up to three individuals per year. Provide concise bullet list.

No tool usage needed.

content:
### Nobel Prize in Physics (2010 – 2015)

| Year | Laureates | Key Contribution |
|------|-----------|------------------|
| **2010** | **Andre Geim** & **Konstantin Novoselov** | Isolated a single‑layer sheet of carbon atoms—**graphene**—and demonstrated its extraordinary mechanical, electrical, and thermal properties, opening a new field of two‑dimensional materials science. |
| **2011** | **Saul Perlmutter**, **Brian P. Schmidt**, **Adam G. Riess** | Used distant type‑Ia supernovae to discover that the expansion of the Universe is accelerating, implying the existence of a repulsive “dark energy” that dominates the cosmic energy budget. |
| **2012** | **Steven Chu**, **Claude Cohen‑Tannoudji**, **William D. Phillips** | Developed laser‑cooling and magnetic‑trap techniques that allow atoms to be cooled to near absolute zero, enabling precision measurements, quantum‑state control, and the creation of Bose‑Einstein condensates. |
| **2013** | **François Englert**, **Peter W. Higgs** | Provided the theoretical framework (the Higgs mechanism) that explains how elementary particles acquire mass, and confirmed the existence of the Higgs boson in 2012 at the Large Hadron Collider. |
| **2014** | **Isamu Akasaki**, **Hiroshi Amano**, **Shuji Nakamura** | Invented blue‑light‑emitting diodes (LEDs) using gallium nitride, which enabled efficient white‑light LEDs and revolutionized lighting, displays, and information technology. |
| **2015** | **Takaaki Kajita**, **Arthur B. McDonald** | Discovered neutrino oscillations, proving that neutrinos have mass and that the three known neutrino flavors mix, thus extending the Standard Model of particle physics. |

These laureates collectively advanced our understanding of condensed matter, cosmology, quantum optics, particle physics, and materials science, each achievement having wide‑ranging scientific and technological impacts.
